name: al-Mutanabbi
bio: Abu al-Tayyib Ahmad ibn al-Husayn was born in Kufa in 303 AH (915 CE) and grew up there and among the desert tribes, where he mastered the language. As a young man he claimed to be a prophet among the tribes of al-Samawa and was jailed for it; the name al-Mutanabbi, “the would-be prophet”, stayed with him after he recanted. From 337 AH (948 CE) he spent nine years with Sayf al-Dawla, the Hamdanid prince of Aleppo, writing his most famous praise poems and the battle poems of the prince's wars with Byzantium. He then went to Kafur, the ruler of Egypt, whom he satirised after leaving, and on to Iraq and Persia, and was killed on his way back to Baghdad, near Dayr al-Aqul, in 354 AH (965 CE). More of his lines became proverbs than almost any other Arabic poet's, and commentators argued over his poems for centuries.
